## Overview

**npdar** provides R utilities for the [National Paediatric Diabetes
Audit (NPDA)](https://www.rcpch.ac.uk/work-we-do/clinical-audits/npda),
developed and maintained by the [Royal College of Paediatrics and Child
Health (RCPCH)](https://www.rcpch.ac.uk/).

The package supports:

-   **Blood pressure assessment:** calculate expected values, z-scores
    and percentiles, and categorise blood pressure using paediatric or
    adult references.

-   **Statistical utilities:**

    1.  mask small counts and apply secondary suppression to reduce the
        risk of back-calculation for data privacy;

    2.  identify first/last/most recent modal values or first/last entry
        in a longitudinal record with options to ignore specific values;

    3.  summarise categorical measure(s) by group(s) with counts,
        denominators and percentages in long format for easy use in
        `ggplot2` and `plotly`.

-   **Audit period identification:** identify audit/fiscal years and
    quarters using a configurable first-quarter start month.

-   **Correlation visualisation:** create interactive correlation matrix
    with `plotly` and `stats::cor()`.

See the [package documentation](https://rcpch.github.io/npdar/) for full
function references and examples.

## Disclaimer :warning:

**This package is designed for:**

-   Assisting NPDA data analysis.
-   Improving transparency and reproducibility of NPDA analysis.
-   Helping other research and epidemiological analysis.

**This package is NOT:**

-   A clinical decision support or diagnosis tool.
-   Approved for use in clinical care pathways.

Healthcare professionals must use validated clinical tools and their
professional judgement when making patient care decisions. The blood
pressure categorisation functions implement published research
guidelines (NHBPEP Fourth Report, NICE/BHF guidances) **for audit
analysis purposes only, not for clinical use**.

## Installation

**npdar** is not currently available on CRAN. Install the development
version from GitHub using [pak](https://pak.r-lib.org/):

```{r}
#| label: install-pak
#| eval: FALSE
install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("rcpch/npdar")

# devtools::install_github() was deprecated 
# in favour of pak::pak() since devtools 2.5.0
# install.packages("devtools")
# devtools::install_github("rcpch/npdar")
```

Alternatively, use [remotes](https://remotes.r-lib.org/):

```{r}
#| label: install-remotes
#| eval: FALSE
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("rcpch/npdar")
```

## Quick Start

```{r}
#| label: load-npdar
library(npdar)
```

### Blood Pressure

It's recommended to use the NHBPEP Fourth Report reference for children
and adolescents aged 0-17 years. Height must already be expressed as a
z-score, not in centimetres or other units. `bp_assess()` returns a tibble with the
expected BP, z-score, percentile and category. The 25-year-old below is
outside this reference's age range, so returns `NA`.

```{r}
#| label: bp-assess-children
bp_assess(
  bp_value = c(95, 125, 155),
  bp_type = "systolic",
  sex = c(1, 2, 1),
  male_code = 1, female_code = 2,
  height_z = c(0, 0.5, -0.5),
  age_years = c(10, 15, 25),
  ref = "Fourth Report"
)
```

For adults older than 17 years, it's recommended to select the NICE/BHF
reference explicitly. Ages outside the selected reference range return
`NA`, and only `category` is defined for adults.

```{r}
#| label: bp-assess-adults
bp_assess(
  bp_value = c(155, 155),
  bp_type = "systolic",
  sex = c(1, 1),
  male_code = 1, female_code = 2,
  height_z = c(0, 0),
  age_years = c(15, 25),
  ref = "NICE/BHF"
)
```

Apart from the `bp_assess()` function, `bp_category()`, `bp_relative()`, 
and `bp_expected()` can be used separately to compute only the category, 
z score, percentile, or expected value respectively.

```{r}
#| label: bp-category-adults
bp_category(
  bp_value = c(155, 155),
  bp_type = "systolic",
  sex = c(1, 1),
  male_code = 1, female_code = 2,
  height_z = c(0, 0),
  age_years = c(15, 25),
  ref = "NICE/BHF",
  .quiet = TRUE
)
```

The `bp_family` functions can be used in a `dplyr` pipeline nicely.

```{r}
#| label: bp-relative-children
df <- data.frame(
  id = 1:3,
  sex = c(1, 2, 1),
  height_z = c(0, 0.5, -0.5),
  age_years = c(10, 15, 25),
  sbp = c(95, 125, 155)
)

df |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    sbp_z = bp_relative(
      bp_value = sbp, bp_type = "systolic",
      sex = sex, 
      male_code = 1, female_code = 2,
      height_z = height_z, 
      age_years = age_years,
      ref = "Fourth",
      .quiet = FALSE)$zscore
  )
```

### Privacy Masking

`get_masked()` masks positive counts below `threshold` which you must specify:
the right value depends on your reporting rules and the NPDA usually uses 3.
By default, zeros and `NA`s are exempt from masking as they are usally
meaningful and do not put privacy at risk, but you can choose to mask them too.
At least two values are always masked, so that a masked count cannot be back-calculated 
from the denominator: if fewer are masked, the next smallest positive value is
masked as well. 
The result is always a character vector, so it can be combined with a mask label. 
The default `mask_label` is "masked" for the masked values. 

```{r}
#| label: mask-default
vec1 <- c(5, 6, 4, 5, 1, 0, 0, NA)
get_masked(vec1, threshold = 3)
```

Customise the threshold and mask label:

```{r}
#| label: mask-threshold-label
get_masked(vec1, threshold = 6, mask_label = "*")
```

Use `mask_zero` and `mask_na` to mask zeros and `NA`s too. At least one
positive value is still masked, otherwise the denominator would reveal
that every masked value is zero or unknown:

```{r}
#| label: mask-zero-na
get_masked(vec1, threshold = 3, mask_label = "*", mask_zero = TRUE)
get_masked(vec1, threshold = 3, mask_label = "*", mask_na = TRUE)
get_masked(vec1, threshold = 3, mask_label = "*", mask_zero = TRUE, mask_na = TRUE)
```

### Longitudinal Summaries

`get_ultimate()` uses vector order, so sort longitudinal records
chronologically before selecting a most recent value. These examples
exclude unknown and missing values and deliberately include tied modes;
warnings explain which modes were not selected.

```{r}
#| label: data-longitudinal
dat_long <- c("A", "B", "C", "A", "A", "Unknown", "Unknown",
              NA, "C", "C", "B", "B", "Unknown",
              NA, NA, NA)
```

Select the tied mode that occurs most recently:

```{r}
#| label: ultimate-recent-mode
get_ultimate(dat_long, find = "uptodate_mode", exclude = "Unknown", na.rm = TRUE)
```

Use the package's `last_mode` rule instead:

```{r}
#| label: ultimate-last-mode
get_ultimate(dat_long, find = "last_mode", exclude = "Unknown", na.rm = TRUE)
```

`NA`s are removed by default. Use `na.rm = FALSE` to treat `NA` as a
meaningful value, e.g. when later visits were deliberately left unknown:

```{r}
#| label: ultimate-na-rm
get_ultimate(dat_long, find = "uptodate_mode", exclude = "Unknown", na.rm = FALSE)
```

### Categorical Frequencies

The following examples use synthetic data. `get_frequency()` returns a
long table with a numerator, denominator and proportion (`percent`, on a
0-1 scale) for each category. Missing measure values are excluded by
default; use `count_na = TRUE` to include them.

```{r}
#| label: data-frequency
set.seed(1999)
dat_survey1 <- data.frame(
  participant_id = seq_len(60),
  country = rep(c("England", "Wales"), each = 30),
  region = rep(
    c("East England", "West England", NA, "North Wales", "South Wales", NA),
    each = 10
  ),
  q1_catq = sample(c("A", "B", "C", NA), 60, replace = TRUE),
  q2_catq = sample(c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", NA), 60, replace = TRUE)
)

dat_survey2 <- data.frame(
  auditYear = c(rep(2021, 3), rep(2022, 3), rep(2023, 6)),
  sex = c(
    "Female", "Female", "Male", "Female", "Male", "Male",
    "Female", "Male", "Male", "Male", NA, NA
  ),
  type = c("A", "B", "B", "A", "B", NA,
           sample(c("A", "B", NA), 6, replace = TRUE))
)
```

#### Separate Group Summary

With `nested = FALSE` (the default), each grouping variable is
summarised separately. The special group name `"overall"` adds an
overall summary.

```{r}
#| label: frequency-example1
sum_freq_eg1 <- get_frequency(
  data = dat_survey1,
  measures = c("q1_catq", "q2_catq"),
  groups = c("overall", "country", "region")
)

sum_freq_eg1 |>
  dplyr::filter(category == "A")
```

#### Nested Group Summary

Use `nested = TRUE` to summarise combinations of grouping variables,
such as sex within each audit year:

```{r}
#| label: frequency-example2
get_frequency(
  data = dat_survey2,
  measures = "type",
  groups = c("auditYear", "sex"),
  nested = TRUE
)
```

#### Count NAs

Use `count_na = TRUE` to include missing values in the denominator and
report them as a separate `NA` category (only for measures that contain
missing values).

```{r}
#| label: frequency-example3
sum_freq_eg3 <- get_frequency(
  data = dat_survey1,
  measures = "q1_catq",
  groups = c("country", "region"),
  nested = TRUE,
  count_na = TRUE
)

sum_freq_eg3 |>
  dplyr::filter(region %in% c("East England", "North Wales"))
```

#### Static Plot with `ggplot2`

```{r}
#| label: frequency-ggplot
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| eval: FALSE
library(ggplot2)

sum_freq_eg1 |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(country)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = country, y = percent, fill = category)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Country", y = "Percent", fill = "Category")
```

#### Interactive Plot with `plotly`

```{r}
#| label: frequency-plotly
#| eval: FALSE
library(plotly)

sum_freq_eg1 |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(country)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(measure) |>
  dplyr::group_map(\(df, ...) {
    plot_ly(df, x = ~country, y = ~percent, 
            color = ~category, type = "bar")
  }) |>
  subplot(nrows = 1, shareX = TRUE, shareY = TRUE)
```

### Audit Periods

The default audit year starts in April. With no date supplied,
`audit_year()` uses today's date:

```{r}
#| label: audit-current
audit_year()
```

Fixed dates keep the rendered examples reproducible:

```{r}
#| label: audit-fixed-date
audit_year("2025-03-31")
audit_year("2025-03-31", format = FALSE)
```

Change the first-quarter start month for a different audit calendar:

```{r}
#| label: audit-custom-start
audit_year("2025-03-31", start_month = 1)
```

Generate an inclusive sequence of audit years:

```{r}
#| label: audit-sequence
data.frame(
  audit_year = audit_year_range(2010, 2015),
  audit_year_numeric = audit_year_range(2010, 2015, format = FALSE)
)
```

### Correlation Matrix with `plotly`

`plot_corrmat_ly()` creates an interactive lower-triangle correlation
heatmap. Supply a data frame containing only numeric variables:

```{r}
#| label: correlation-basic
#| eval: FALSE
plot_corrmat_ly(mtcars)
```

Customise the plot, for example by selecting Spearman correlations,
hiding the values and customising the colour bar:

```{r}
#| label: correlation-custom
#| eval: FALSE
plot_corrmat_ly(
  mtcars,
  method = "spearman",
  show_values = FALSE,
  show_stars = TRUE,
  colorbar = list(title = "Spearman Corr")
) |>
  plotly::layout(
    margin = list(b = 80),
    annotations = list(list(
      text = paste0("<i><b>Note:</b> *: p<0.05, **: p<0.01, ***: p<0.001.</i>"),
      x = 1, y = -0.15, xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
      xanchor = "right", yanchor = "top",
      showarrow = FALSE
    ))
  )
```

### Raincloud Plot with `plotly`

`plot_raincloud_ly()` creates an interactive raincloud plot, combining a
half-violin density, a boxplot and the raw data points for each group. The
orientation follows the data: a numeric `x` with a categorical `y` gives a
horizontal plot, and the reverse gives a vertical one.

```{r}
#| label: raincloud-basic
#| eval: FALSE
set.seed(1)
plot_raincloud_ly(iris,
                  x = "Species",
                  y = "Sepal.Length",
                  scatter_layout = "jitter",
                  show_buttons = FALSE)
```

Buttons below the plot show or hide the density, scatter and box elements.
Customise the plot, for example by using a vertical layout with custom colours,
stacked dots instead of jitter, no boxplot and a legend, and tweak it further
with `plotly::layout()`:

```{r}
#| label: raincloud-custom
#| eval: FALSE
plot_raincloud_ly(iris,
                  x = "Sepal.Length",
                  y = "Species",
                  colors = c("#11A7F2", "#E00087", "#00bdaa"),
                  scatter_layout = "dots",
                  show_box = FALSE,
                  show_legend = TRUE) |>
  plotly::layout(yaxis = list(showticklabels = FALSE),
                 legend = list(x = 1, y = -0.2, xanchor = "right",
                               orientation = "h"))
```
